stances.claim: Sampaloc did not produce future Chief Justices -- it produced workers, survivors, children who learned early that hunger was not an event but a condition.
stances.rhetorical_move: rebuttal-of-future-greatness opening + workers-survivors-children triplet + hunger-as-condition-not-event aphorism

stances.claim: In a cramped rented apartment on Cataluña Street, the youngest of four children grew up listening to adult conversations about money that never stretched far enough -- his father Artemio Sr. had left school early to support seven younger siblings after the death of his own father; his mother Patricia Villaseñor had little formal education but possessed the quiet endurance common to women who carry families through scarcity.

He sold newspapers before dawn, he sold cigarettes during the day, he learned which streets produced buyers and which produced trouble -- some nights it made no sense to go home; he slept on sidewalks, not from neglect but from calculation: the papers arrived early, he needed to be there first.
It was here, long before law books or Latin maxims, that Art learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later.

School became refuge -- he studied not because teachers praised him, but because excellence was the only escape route he could see; he graduated with honors from Juan Luna Elementary and Victorino Mapa High, rising in crowded classrooms where obscurity was the default fate.
stances.rhetorical_move: school-as-refuge framing + excellence-as-escape-route motive + obscurity-as-default-fate background

stances.claim: When he was accepted to the University of the Philippines on scholarship it seemed that fate had finally cracked open -- then came the bus fare. Fifteen centavos. That was the distance between Sampaloc and Diliman -- between promise and possibility. He never complained. He simply walked to Far Eastern University instead.

one_paragraph_summary: Art's childhood-of-origin chapter, anchored in a cramped rented apartment on Cataluña Street, Sampaloc, where the youngest of four children grew up with a father (Artemio Sr.) who had left school early to support seven younger siblings after his own father's death, and a mother (Patricia Villaseñor) of little formal education but quiet endurance. The boy sold newspapers before dawn and cigarettes during the day, sleeping on sidewalks not from neglect but from calculation (the papers arrived early), recalling those nights later 'without sentimentality' -- 'the cold stone beneath his back' and 'the envy he refused to indulge' when he imagined classmates sleeping in beds. Here, 'long before law books or Latin maxims,' he learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later. School became refuge -- he graduated with honors from Juan Luna Elementary and Victorino Mapa High, then was accepted to UP on scholarship, only to be foreclosed by a fifteen-centavo bus fare that was 'the distance between Sampaloc and Diliman, between promise and possibility.' He never complained -- he simply walked to Far Eastern University instead.
